title: Demographic representation of COVID-19 social media and information engagement in Nigeria
screen_reason: Cross-sectional online survey of 1127 Nigerian adults (June 2020) reporting quantitative shares of respondents with a stated denominator: 93.1% (1049/1127) who received COVID-19 misinformation via social media (self-reported exposure = RECALL exposure) and 12.3% (130/1061) who shared the unverified/speculative protection information with personal contacts (RECALL sharing). Both are descriptive shares of respondents, so the paper qualifies even though its stated aim is demographic engagement patterns.

estimates.platform: Social media (Twitter, Facebook, WhatsApp, Instagram, YouTube)
estimates.measure_type: % of survey respondents who reported receiving misinformation about the COVID-19 pandemic through social media
estimates.denominator: 1127 adults aged >=18 years resident in Nigeria who completed an online (Google Form) cross-sectional survey
estimates.definition: Respondent answered that they had received misinformation about the COVID-19 pandemic through social media; no external verification of the content, the respondent classifies it
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition given; misinformation is illustrated as 'speculative information on protection against COVID-19 through social media platforms, for example, the use of chloroquine, hot water, bleach, and herbal remedies'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent self-report in an anonymous online Google Form survey; no external coding, no fact-check benchmark and no reliability statistics reported
estimates.moderator_quote: A cross-sectional online survey, using Google Form, was used to collect data related to the spread of COVID-19 information in June 2020. Eligible participants were adults aged >=18 years residing in Nigeria. Data on demography, information source, media consumption patterns, and information accuracy and responsibility were collected through snowballing technique and promoted through emails and social networking sites.
estimates.notes: Headline self-reported exposure figure. Denominator is the full sample (1127), unlike the 'action taken' items which use 1061. Recruitment was snowball/online promotion, so the sample is highly educated (92.1% undergraduate or above) and not population-representative. estimates.measure_type: % of survey respondents who said they shared the speculative COVID-19 cure/protection information they received with personal contacts on social platforms without verifying it
estimates.denominator: 1061 respondents who answered the item on action taken on information received about a cure for COVID-19
estimates.definition: Respondent selected 'Shared it with personal contacts using social platforms' as the action taken on the speculative COVID-19 cure/protection information they had received, i.e. passed it on without checking its validity
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition given; the content in question is 'speculative information on protection against COVID-19 ... for example, the use of chloroquine, hot water, bleach, and herbal remedies'
estimates.page_loc: Results, p.2; Table 1, 'Action taken on information received for cure to COVID-19 (n=1061)', row 'Shared it with personal contacts using social platforms (n=130)'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent self-report; the content shared is described by the authors as 'speculative' unverified protection/cure advice rather than externally verified falsehood; no reliability statistics
estimates.moderator_quote: Most participants received speculative information on protection against COVID-19 through social media platforms, for example, the use of chloroquine, hot water, bleach, and herbal remedies. About 59.7% (633/1061) checked the validity of the information received on authorized platforms, such as the World Health Organization website.
estimates.notes: borderline=true: the shared material is unverified/speculative COVID-19 cure advice rather than content confirmed false against an external ground truth, so this is a self-reported sharing-of-suspect-content share rather than a clean misinformation-sharing share. Kept because the paper's own framing treats this stream as misinformation and the numerator/denominator are stated verbatim. missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) 82.9% (934/1127) who 'believed social media was the primary source of inaccurate information' - this is an attribution of blame to a channel, not a share of respondents exposed to or sharing misinformation, so it is not a prevalence estimate; (b) 22.2% (248/1118) who considered information accurate 'because the source constantly bears correct news' and the other 'information accuracy check' items - these are verification heuristics, not exposure; (c) 5.9% (63/1061) who 'Tried out some of the recommendations' and 5.5% (58/1061) who 'Believed it' - these are belief/behaviour outcomes, explicitly excluded; (d) 59.7% (633/1061) who checked credible sources - a verification behaviour; (e) all demographic breakdowns in Table 1 (by age, gender, education) - per the collapse rule the headline figures are kept rather than subgroup rows, and demographics are not the paper's headline construct. No definition-variant rows exist: misinformation is never operationalised more or less strictly.

rob.design: Cross-sectional online survey (Google Form), June 2020, adults >=18 resident in Nigeria; non-probability snowball sampling promoted via email and social networking sites, so no sampling frame and no response rate can be computed; n=1127 with item-level denominators varying (1061-1127); all measures are single-item self-reports analysed with descriptive statistics in Stata 16; no coding procedure, no inter-rater reliability and no external validation of what respondents counted as misinformation; sample skewed to the highly educated (92.1% undergraduate or above) and authors concede 'the online recruitment strategy may have limited respondent variety'.
rob.item6_quote: Most participants received speculative information on protection against COVID-19 through social media platforms, for example, the use of chloroquine, hot water, bleach, and herbal remedies.
rob.item10_quote: Overall, 93.1% (1049/1127) received misinformation about the pandemic through social media, and 82.9% (934/1127) believed social media was the primary source of inaccurate information.
